https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: People rest on a beach under the supervision of Guardia Civil officers in Ceuta on Saturday. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images View image in fullscreen People rest on a beach under the supervision of Guardia Civil officers in Ceuta on Saturday. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Spain Chaos of border crossing gives way to limbo for Moroccans on Ceuta’s streets People among the more than 50,000 who entered Spanish enclave this week describe the journey and their prospects Okba Mohammad and Javier Jennings Mozo in Ceuta Sun 2 Aug 2026 09.11 EDT Last modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 13.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google F our days ago, Youssef El Abbas saw an opportunity to reclaim the life he had lost seven years earlier. News was circulating that about 400 people had swum from Morocco to the neighbouring Spanish enclave of Ceuta on the north African coast, approximately 12 miles (19km) across the strait of Gibraltar from mainland Spain. Here was a chance for the 44-year-old Moroccan father of four to return to Spain , from which he had been deported when his residency expired after the loss of his job in Bilbao in 2019. El Abbas took a taxi and headed to the city of Tétouan, south of the enclave. While en route, he saw Facebook posts and news reports claiming that the Moroccan authorities were allowing people to pass through their side of the border. That meant that unlike those who had crossed the previous night, he could simply travel overland before swimming for just five minutes across the border from Moroccan to Spanish territory to avoid the Spanish border controls. View image in fullscreen People returning to Morocco on Sunday after crossing into Ceuta. Photograph: Reduan Dris/EPA He reached Tétouan to find the city completely overwhelmed. “Young men were running through the streets, flooding every corner,” he said. By the time a second taxi took El Abbas to Fnideq, the town bordering Ceuta, he realised that the usual blockades and checkpoints preventing people without European documents from even approaching the frontier had been removed. View image in fullscreen Youssef El Abbas in Ceuta. Photograph: Okba Mohammad “The Moroccan police were shouting at us: ‘Go, go, go! Run now, run into Spain,’” he said. “The night before, they were beating people. But that morning they were letting us through. Nothing made sense.” Despite the crowds, El Abbas noticed the police were only letting Moroccans cross over. “All the sub-Saharan migrants were being pushed back by force.” He reached the border at 2.45pm on Wednesday. By 3pm, after a short swim, he was standing on Spanish soil. Not everyone was so lucky. “In just 10 minutes in the water, I saw four people floating dead in Moroccan waters,” he said. “People were pulling their bodies out.” They were among at least 72 people who drowned or were crushed trying to reach the Spanish territory. El Abbas is just one of the 50,000 or so people to have crossed into Ceuta this week , in what Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, described as “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity”. Map showing location of Ceuta between Morocco and Spain, and another map showing line of Morocco-Ceuta border and Tarajal breakwater Madrid has attributed the latest influx to “human-trafficking mafias” that have taken advantage of a decision by Spain’s supreme court, which recently ruled that those intercepted at sea while trying to enter Ceuta or Melilla – the other Spanish enclave on the north African coast – could not be summarily returned under special rules. The same hand that helped me out of the water was the one that later hit me But there has also been speculation that the Moroccan authorities may have opened the border to signal their displeasure at Sánchez’s recent visit to Algeria, which supports efforts to free the disputed territory of Western Sahara from Moroccan occupation. Morocco’s ambassador to Spain, Karima Benyaich Millán, said Rabat was not happy about the mass crossing, adding that it hoped those in Ceuta would return. Moroccan government sources told the Europa Press news agency that the surge of people entering Ceuta was down to “criminal organisations” and insisted that Rabat’s cooperation with Spain remained “exemplary”. In May 2021, Rabat loosened border controls – allowing 10,000 people to cross into Ceuta over the course of two days – during a diplomatic standoff triggered after Madrid allowed a Western Sahara independence leader to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain. View image in fullscreen A man bends down to pick up a pair of shoes from debris washed up on Ceuta’s shore. Photograph: Pedro Nunes/Reuters El Abbas said he had never stopped dreaming of returning to Spain, where he had worked mainly in the hospitality sector for 14 years. Since being deported to Morocco in 2019, he has lived apart from his wife and four daughters, who remain in the northern Spanish city of Bilbao, while scraping by with occasional work repairing mobile phones alongside his father. “I never stopped thinking about coming back,” he said. “In Morocco, I was alive, but I wasn’t really living.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day Preview latest after newsletter promotion Why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint and how were so many people able to cross from Morocco? Read more The return has been bittersweet. When he swam ashore in Ceuta, a Spanish Guardia Civil officer extended a hand to pull him from the sea. But that gesture of aid eventually gave way to one of violence. Three days after arriving, the group of people he was with were surrounded by a military patrol and beaten. “The same hand that helped me out of the water was the one that later hit me,” he said. El Abbas’s story is hardly unique. Although more than 48,000 people had crossed back into Morocco by Friday night, hundreds are still sleeping in parks, public squares and on pavements, waiting for a chance to move on or simply to find somewhere to rest. It appears to be virtually impossible for migrants to leave Ceuta for mainland Spain. Said, 17, from Casablanca, was sitting on a kerb a few hundred metres away. He, too, had joined the Ceuta-bound crowds when he heard that the border was open. But the jubilation had given way to reality and all he had was a bottle of water and the carton of yoghurt a local resident had given him. 3:37 Tens of thousands of migrants cross into Spanish enclave Ceuta from Morocco - video The teenager said he was taken to a centre for unaccompanied minors after he crossed, but there were no places available, so he ended up back on the streets. According to a soldier who asked to remain anonymous, the current protocol for the authorities – including the military, the police and the Guardia Civil – is to treat unaccompanied minors as regular migrants and return them to Morocco. Said and the other teenagers with him said no one would sell them food or allow them into shops and restaurants because they did not speak Spanish. Three days after the mass influx, Ceuta is slowly trying to recover a sense of normality. By early evening on Saturday, cafe terraces were beginning to fill again and some businesses had reopened their doors. Many of the remaining arrivals are being tended to by Ceuta locals, who walk the streets handing out bottles of water, sandwiches, blankets and clothes. Others stop to ask if they need help or to offer to call a relative. Such shows of solidarity have been threatened by the arrival of far-right politicians and a neo-Nazi group, all keen to use the humanitarian crisis for their own ends. “They’re going to exploit our feelings to claim the credit and say they defended Ceuta,” said a local woman called Malika. “We don’t want them here. If they want to defend something, they should go somewhere else.” View image in fullscreen People who crossed into Ceuta this week are escorted back to Morocco by the Spanish army on Saturday. Photograph: Antonio Sempere/AP Malika, who was born in Ceuta to a soldier who served in the Spanish army, rejected the notion that the city should be defined solely by the political confrontation that followed this week’s mass arrival. But she also acknowledged the pressure on a city of just over 80,000 people. “It would have been an impossible situation for any city,” she said. Fatima Hamed Hossain, a member of Ceuta’s assembly, fears that the strain created by the crisis has deepened divisions within the city. “Everything we’ve lived through has created tensions between neighbours,” she said. “That’s exactly what feeds the far right.” As a caravan of people returned back over the border, Said’s mind was on the future. His goal is simple: get a place in a protection centre, spend the next year learning Spanish and, once he turns 18, find work as a barber. What he fears most is ending up without legal documentation and seeing that plan collapse before it has even begun. Leaving is not on his agenda, however. “All I need,” he said, “is a chance.” Explore more on these topics Spain Morocco Migration Africa Europe Middle East and north Africa news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.carlow-nationalist.ie/opinio.text: Sun, 02 Aug, 2026 - 09:53 Fr Paddy Byrne: The enduring courage and compassion of the Ulma family Stock image of two people holding hands in compassion       Fr Paddy Byrne The Ulma family showed extraordinary compassion and bravery in the direst situations I WAS greatly inspired recently by the story of the Ulma family, patrons of family life and the unborn child. In a world overshadowed by terror and brutality, the story of Józef and Wiktoria Ulma and their six young children shines as a beacon of humanity and moral clarity. Living in the quiet village of Markowa in southeastern Poland during the dark years of the Holocaust, the Ulmas epitomised the extraordinary courage of ordinary people. Risking everything, they sheltered eight Jewish neighbours in their modest home, defying the oppressive machinery of Nazi Germany. Their ultimate sacrifice - losing their lives and those of their children - stands as a profound testament to the power of empathy and faith in the face of unimaginable danger. Józef and Wiktoria Ulma were beacons of resilience, intellect and humanity. Their lives, though marked by simplicity, were extraordinary in their depth and purpose. Józef, born in 1900, was a man of immense curiosity and practical genius. He transcended his humble beginnings. His interests were vast, ranging from horticulture to photography. Wiktoria, born in 1912, was equally remarkable. Orphaned at a young age, she displayed resilience and a zest for life, attending courses at a local folk high school and engaging in cultural activities like village theatre. Together, the Ulmas created a household filled with love, learning and faith. Parents to six children and expecting a seventh, their lives revolved around nurturing not only their family but also their community. Before the second World War, Markowa was a quiet, close-knit community of about 4,500 residents, including around 120 Jews. While cultural and religious differences meant that Polish and Jewish residents lived somewhat parallel lives, relations were amicable. Jewish families in Markowa primarily engaged in trade and farming, their children attending schools alongside Polish peers. Religious gatherings often took place in nearby ÅaÅcut, at a synagogue that likely welcomed the Goldman family - the very neighbours the Ulmas would later risk everything to protect. The peaceful life of the Ulmas and their neighbours was shattered with the German invasion of Poland in 1939. For the Jewish community of Markowa, the occupation brought swift and devastating oppression. Early restrictions, such as wearing the Star of David, escalated into forced labour, deportations and mass executions. By 1942, Operation Reinhardt sought to exterminate the Jewish population in the general government area, leaving Jewish families in Markowa desperate for refuge. Markowa fell under the jurisdiction of brutal German and local collaborators. Daily life became a litany of terror: curfews, forced labour and deportations were commonplace. The Jewish residents, targeted with relentless persecution, were subjected to confiscations, ghettoisation and ultimately, extermination. The Ulmas, known for their kindness and connection to local Jewish families, did not hesitate. In December 1942, they opened their modest home to eight Jews: Saul Goldman, his four sons, two daughters and a young child. For over a year, these individuals lived hidden within the Ulmas’ home, sharing the family’s meagre resources. Such an act of defiance carried the ultimate risk; under the German Nazi decrees, anyone aiding Jews faced immediate execution, a punishment that extended to entire households. In the early hours of 24 March 1944, German gendarmes and local collaborators arrived at the Ulma home. The brutality was swift and unrelenting. The eight Jewish individuals hiding in the house were executed immediately. Józef and Wiktoria were then dragged outside and shot. As Wiktoria fell, in the throes of childbirth, the executioners made a harrowing decision: they would kill the children too. The Ulmas were guided by an unshakable faith. Their well-worn bible contained underlined passages from the parable of the Good Samaritan and the commandment to love one’s neighbour, reflecting the principles that shaped their actions. Their choice to shelter Jews was an act of profound moral courage, rooted in love and a sense of shared humanity. The family’s beatification by the Catholic Church in 2023 underscores their spiritual legacy. While their recognition as Righteous Among the Nations resonates deeply within Jewish memory, their elevation to sainthood amplifies their story on a global scale, reminding Catholics and non-Catholics alike of the universal values they represent compassion, sacrifice and unwavering moral clarity. The Ulma family’s story transcends national and religious boundaries. It is a testament to the enduring power of human dignity in the face of unspeakable evil. The Ulmas stand as symbols of resistance and humanity during one of history’s darkest chapters. Their legacy challenges us to reflect on our own capacity for courage and compassion. Today, as their names appear in museums, textbooks and prayers, the Ulmas remind the world that even in the bleakest times, ordinary people can achieve extraordinary heroism. Their story is not merely one of martyrdom but a beacon of hope. too. In yet another heinous crime, the mullahs’ judiciary hanged brave protester Shahram Sadeghi in Karaj on the morning of Sunday, August 16, 2026. Sadeghi’s execution is part of a broader, systemic wave of state-sponsored killings aimed at terrorizing the public. Yet, these executions only expose the religious dictatorship’s profound fear of an increasingly restive and uncompromising society. Sadeghi was arrested on February 5, 2026, shortly after the peak of the uprisings. On May 30, 2026, the Revolutionary Court of Karaj swiftly sentenced him to death and ordered the confiscation of all his property. To justify the execution, the regime’s judiciary claimed that on the night of January 8, 2026, near Karaj’s Golzar Crossroads, Sadeghi drove his vehicle at high speed, injuring seven regime agents, before allegedly colluding with “rioters” to set his own car on fire. Read more Defying the Dictatorship: Resistance Units Support Simay Azadi Telethon with 30 Daring Operations In a display of support for the 30th national telethon of Simay Azadi (Iran National Television – INTV), PMOI/MEK Resistance Units carried out 30 daring operations against regime targets across Iran. INTV serves as the true voice of the Iranian people and remains the only network that broadcasts the operations and activities of the Resistance Units. Sending a powerful message to the telethon, the Resistance Units declared: “We, the Resistance Units inside Iran, have no money, but we sacrifice everything for Iran.” The nationwide campaign spanned major cities and provinces, including Aligudarz, Isfahan, Kermanshah, Mashhad, Shiraz, Azna, Birjand, Iranshahr, Khorramabad, Nikshahr, Semirom, Shahriyar, Tehran, and Zahedan. The Resistance Units took direct aim at the regime’s apparatus of terror, targeting and setting fire to IRGC Basij bases—which are primarily tasked with spying on and suppressing dissidents—in Isfahan, Kermanshah, Mashhad, and Iranshahr. They also set fire to regime facilities, including a regime building in Aligudarz and the local headquarters of the Khomeini Foundation in Shiraz. Shattering the regime’s image of authority, the Resistance Units systematically torched state propaganda posters. This included setting fire to posters of regime founder Ruhollah Khomeini, the eliminated former supreme leader Ali Khamenei, and the new regime supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei. Read more Iran: Women at Fardis Prison Surrounded by Sewage and Exposed to Disease The sanitary conditions in Hall 1 of Fardis Prison in Karaj are extremely poor. Prisoners in this ward are exposed to sewage and are facing serious health risks. In the recreation area of Hall 1, sewage has overflowed and covered the entire area used by prisoners. The sewage has accumulated on the ground like a lake throughout the area, while prison authorities have taken no action to address the problem, despite the summer heat. The smell of sewage and contaminated air has attracted insects. Prisoners are unable to use the recreation area, and the conditions have led to various illnesses. Many prisoners have developed illnesses, including diarrhea and vomiting, as a result of the problem. The prison medical unit has also taken no action to treat the affected women prisoners. Some of the women held in this prison are political prisoners . Read more Iran’s Medicine Shortage Deepens as Regime Mismanagement Fuels a Growing Health Crisis Iran’s medicine shortage has evolved far beyond the temporary absence of a few specialized drugs from pharmacy shelves. In 2026, statements by officials, field reports, and warnings from health-sector professionals reveal a multilayered crisis involving disruptions in foreign-currency allocation and raw-material supplies, massive insurance debts, severe liquidity shortages among pharmaceutical producers and pharmacies, weaknesses in distribution and oversight, and the emergence of a parallel market where medicines unavailable through official channels are sold at exorbitant prices. The crisis increasingly reflects the responsibility of the Iranian regime’s economic and health policies, rather than an unavoidable shortage caused solely by external circumstances. Even official figures on the scale of medicine shortages are contradictory. On August 3, 2026, the head of the Food and Drug Administration said the number of essential medicines classified as being in shortage had fallen from 341 to 65. Read more Iran’s Gasoline Price Test Exposes Regime’s Fear of a New Social Explosion For more than a decade, gasoline prices in Iran have been a political flashpoint. Few economic issues have so consistently threatened to shake government policy and trigger warnings of social unrest. The fundamental imbalance between the Iranian regime and society remains economic hardship and deteriorating living conditions—and gasoline has become one of its most combustible manifestations. Over the past several days, the government quietly tested a sharp increase in gasoline prices. A price of 78,200 tomans per liter was initially announced and then implemented in Kerman. Within hours, however, the governor of Kerman ordered the sale of gasoline at that price halted. The episode triggered warnings from regime officials and experts, many of whom invoked the memory of the November 2019 nationwide uprising, which followed a gasoline-price increase and rapidly became a major political crisis. The sequence—announcement, trial implementation, and rapid suspension—suggests an attempt to measure public reaction. The apparent strategy is to announce an exceptionally high price, provoke resistance, retreat, and then introduce a lower but still significantly increased price. In effect, the government would seek to make a substantial increase appear more acceptable by comparison. Read more Iran’s Banking System Shows Signs of Systemic Distress as Regime Admits Capital Shortfalls and Hidden Bad Loans Iran’s banking system is facing a combination of capital weakness, bad loans, frozen assets, inadequate oversight, and foreign-exchange irregularities, according to an unusually revealing report carried by the regime’s state-run Mehr News Agency. The report quoted Zabihollah Khodaiian, head of the regime’s General Inspection Organization, during a meeting with Central Bank officials, bank executives, banking technology managers, and other government inspectors. While Khodaiian framed the discussion around strengthening the banking system and supporting the economy, his remarks exposed a far more serious picture: a financial system struggling to recover its own resources while being expected to finance production, households, and an economy already under severe pressure. The revelations are particularly significant because they come from inside the regime’s own supervisory apparatus. Read more Iran’s Healthcare Services in Crisis with Shortage of 100,000 Nurses The shortage of 100,000 nurses in Iran’s healthcare system has now become one of the most serious crises facing the country’s medical services. Abbas Ebadi, the Deputy Minister of Health for Nursing Affairs, has also confirmed this figure. At the same time, the Ministry of Health has announced that it needs to recruit 60,000 personnel. However, Iran’s Administrative and Employment Affairs Organization has not yet responded to this request. Abbas Ebadi, the Deputy Minister of Health for Nursing Affairs, spoke on August 14 about the state of the nursing workforce. He said that the Ministry of Health has formally announced its need to recruit new personnel. The request covers the entire healthcare system. However, the Administrative and Employment Affairs Organization has not yet announced the outcome of its review. Read more Iran And the US Are Neither at War nor at Peace — They Are Locked in A “War of Endurance” TEHRAN — Iran-US relations have entered a situation that is difficult to explain through traditional definitions of war and peace. Negotiations continue, Iranian officials are discussing shipping arrangements with Oman, and the possibility of an understanding is still being discussed; at the same time, neither side — Iran nor the United States — has backed away from its core positions in the Strait of Hormuz , and the possibility of renewed attacks has not been removed from political calculations. What has emerged is not a stable ceasefire, but a competition over who can withstand pressure longer and raise the costs for the other side. Babak Negahdari , head of the Iranian parliament’s Research Center, described the situation more explicitly than many Iranian officials. He said one of the enemies’ objectives is to “trap Iran in a state of neither war nor peace ” so that the country “remains constantly engaged, worn down and in conflict with its neighbors,” adding: “This vicious cycle must be broken and the country must emerge from the current state of attrition.” Read more Major Rally in New York on Sept 22 to Stop Executions and Oppose Pezeshkian’s UN Appearance The Organization of Iranian American Communities ( OIAC ) has released an official flyer inviting Iranian Americans and freedom-loving Iranians to a major rally in New York on Tuesday, September 22, 2026. The event will take place at 9:00 a.m. at Dag Hammarskjold Plaza (2nd Ave & 47th St.), opposite the United Nations. Organizers are calling on participants to demand an end to executions and torture in Iran, support women’s resistance and students, and push for democracy. A key message on the flyer states: “Do not allow Pezeshkian to address the United Nations. He does not represent the Iranian people.” Supporters of the Iranian Resistance across the United States, including voices from California and Los Angeles, have amplified the call, urging widespread participation to protest ongoing executions of political prisoners and to stand for a free and democratic Iran. Read more Bucharest Exhibition Calls for Urgent Action to Stop Executions in Iran Bucharest, Romania – August 15, 2026 – Supporters of the Iranian Resistance ( NCRI and PMOI ) held a photo exhibition in Bucharest highlighting human rights violations in Iran and calling for urgent international action to stop the execution of political prisoners and prevent the implementation of death sentences. An exhibition highlighting human rights violations in Iran was held in Bucharest by MEK supporters “Urgent action is needed to stop the execution of political prisoners in Iran,” the exhibition emphasized, drawing attention to the continued detention of protesters arrested during Iran’s January 2026 uprising, as well as the executions and imminent execution of political prisoners. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Nepal-Tibet flood disaster Briton among 119 more people rescued in Nepal after flash floods More than 1,000 people confirmed dead and more than 4,000 still missing in disaster triggered by glacial collapse Angus Thomson Tue 1 Sep 2026 14.48 EDT Last modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 15.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A British national was among 119 people rescued in Nepal on Tuesday, an official said almost a week after deadly flash floods on the country’s border with Tibet. An army spokesperson told reporters at a press conference that Tuesday’s rescue efforts had saved 118 Nepali nationals – 44 women and 74 men. “We have also rescued one British male during this search and rescue operation, and the search and rescue operation is continuing,” he said. The British man is yet to be identified. The UK Foreign Office was contacted for comment. The rescues mark a rare breakthrough in a devastating week for Himalayan communities on both sides of the Nepal-Tibet border. At least 1,050 people have been confirmed dead in Nepal since Wednesday’s flash floods, while Chinese state media said 66 people had been killed in Tibet. More than 4,000 people are still missing. Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, said 11,000 people had been rescued across the affected region. This included 330 foreign nationals, the Nepalese tourist board said in an update on Tuesday. Preliminary analysis of satellite imagery suggests the collapse of a glacier high in the Himalayas was the primary cause of the disaster. How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guide Read more The collapse – so large it was initially recorded as a magnitude-4.4 earthquake – triggered a deadly torrent of water, mud and ice that tore along the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on Wednesday. Crews have faced dangerous and difficult conditions while searching unstable terrain and flood debris. Search efforts are now focused on attempts to reach about 600 workers believed to be trapped inside tunnels at several hydropower stations in the region. “Massive work has been going on in the tunnel, all the tunnels,” the army spokesperson said on Tuesday. Thirty-six British nationals are missing, the Foreign Office minister, Stewart Wood, told the House of Lords on Tuesday. The figure had previously been put at 33. A rapid deployment rescue team from the UK arrived in Nepal on Saturday to provide support for Britons and their families as part of the government’s £5m commitment to support relief and recovery efforts. The Red Cross estimates that 93,000 people have been directly affected by the disaster. Scientists have said such disasters are more likely as the climate crisis affects mountainous and polar regions. The UN’s top scientific advisory body said in 2023 that previously ice-bound landmasses – such as permafrost tundra and mountain glaciers – would become increasingly unstable as temperatures rose . Officials from Nepal, China and Tibet met in May to discuss strengthening their joint response to floods, weather and glacier-related hazards, Reuters reported on Tuesday . Close Share A A A He was polite and well-dressed, the homeless man with a neat, white beard who became a fixture in Nicholson Street, Carlton North. No one remembers when he arrived, but they know when he left. The man, who for years would sweep the driveway and hang his few possessions on hooks in a small alcove protected from the street, was found dead on May 23, 2004. The locals who knew him always wondered where he went every day. He would leave the apartment alcove full of purpose at 9am like any other commuter to catch a city-bound tram and return at 6.30pm. When residents said hello he would not respond. They wondered if he was shy or couldn’t talk. Professor Trevor Lithgow was working at the microbiology department at the University of Melbourne when he moved into the Nicholson Street apartment block in 2002. “The mailboxes were in the alcove, and it became apparent someone was living there. There were cardboard boxes and everything was neatly stacked. “He had a routine, he would pack up his possessions, sweep the driveway, jump on a tram then return and sweep the driveway again. Advertisement “He was our neighbour who happened to be homeless.” The man’s fingerprints were not on record which meant he had no criminal convictions, dental records produced nothing, and the computer-generated image distributed in the media drew a blank. Charity meal stations, hospitals and homeless shelters couldn’t identify him. The poster looking for leads to identify the Alcove Man. He still wore a gold wedding band, which suggested he was not always a loner. Yet, no one had reported him missing. The Alcove Man was destined to be one of the many mysteries of a big city, remembered only as a curiosity by a handful of strangers, if not for experts at the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine, who used cutting-edge DNA technology to embark on a historic journey through seven countries to find the truth. First the experts used DNA to find the man was of Jewish descent. Yet no one in the close Melbourne Jewish community knew him. To understand this journey, we need to first understand the technology. DNA is not a stationary science but one that constantly evolves. Which brings us to Forensic Investigative Genetic Genealogy (FIGG). Advertisement FIGG is to basic DNA what draughts is to chess. “There have been advances in DNA, but this one is a leap,” says the Victorian institute’s forensic DNA intelligence expert, Dr Runa Daniel. That leap is breathing life into cold crime cases. Victoria Police don’t want to talk about it, but they are using FIGG in at least a dozen rape and murder mysteries. There have already been breakthroughs. There will be more. In one case, police have gone back to ancestors in the 1880s to build a family tree of 5500 names involving five generations around the world that they hope will identify a suspect just around the corner from a crime scene. The most celebrated case was California’s Golden State Killer, former US cop Joseph DeAngelo , who pleaded guilty to 13 murders and about 50 rapes after he was identified using FIGG. Joseph James DeAngelo, the Golden State Killer, in court in 2020. AP Law enforcement agencies and forensic teams upload DNA samples into genealogy databases, GEDmatch Pro and FamilyTreeDNA, looking for any matches, then try to build a family tree back to their person of interest. Before anyone screams civil liberties, the samples are only checked against people who have opted in to co-operate on the two databases. Advertisement It was back in 2019 when the forensic medicine institute, the Australia Federal Police and NSW Police conducted a study on the viability of FIGG. They liked what they saw. In 2020, with no leads on the Alcove Man’s identity, the institute began using FIGG to manufacture one, slowly building his family tree from the furthest leaf – a first cousin, once removed, living in America. Editor's pick Naked City ‘Granny Evil’ to some, ‘Nanna Kath’ to others. The matriarch who built a crime empire and inspired a movie This meant they shared one grandparent. It was a start but only that. Through emails and international conversations, the forensic institute’s team of Daniel, chief molecular biologist Dr Dadna Hartman and Dr Colleen Fitzpatrick, an expert genealogical researcher, began to piece together the story that began in Warsaw, Poland, months before the end of World War I. “It began a journey of discovery for all of us,” Hartman says. The experts found leads, bumped into dead ends and looked for evidence in Poland, the US, Israel, Greece, Germany, Italy and Australia. Advertisement Polish couple Yakov Kwiat and Jente Pomerancz had five children. Three boys, Yitzhak, Izrael and Chemia, and two girls. Fitzpatrick concluded there was a 69 per cent probability that one of the brothers was the man in the alcove. As the institute’s team began to build the family tree, they found the sisters, Esther and Kahna, died in the Holocaust. Izrael and Yitzhak migrated to Israel, while Chemia, by now a professional tailor, proved himself to be resilient, resourceful and lucky to survive World War II. Part of the paper trail in the investigation to identify the man who died in Carlton North. National Archives He was 21 when the Nazis invaded Poland, and lived for three years in a ghetto before being part of a 1942 mass deportation of Polish Jews for extermination. Somehow he survived the Holocaust, massive aerial bombardments and invasions by the Soviets and the Allies. The Nazis killed 6 million Jews, of which 3 million were from Poland. Of the 3.3 million Polish Jews, only 300,000 survived. Chemia lived a further two years in post-war Germany before moving to Italy in 1947 and finding his way to the overcrowded Bagnoli refugee camp in Naples that housed 10,000 people trying to flee to the US, Australia, Canada, Argentina and Israel. Advertisement He was issued passport No.150472 in Bagnoli, on August 18, 1949. His photo showed a neat, well-dressed man, with a slightly receding hairline and an optimistic smile. Using cutting-edge DNA technology, the homeless man was identified as Chemia Kwiat. National Archives He sailed to Australia in October 1949 on the Anna Salen, a refugee transport ship that was a pre-war cargo vessel later converted to the Royal Navy aircraft carrier escort HMS Archer. It made six trips to Australia, bringing thousands of migrants. This voyage was its third. On this journey, many disembarked in Fremantle due to illness brought with them from the camp. Some died on board. Chemia continued to Melbourne. “We found it was a long, tough journey for Mr Kwiat to get to Australia,” Daniel says. It took him 10 years and he travelled 2225 kilometres by land and 30,000 kilometres by sea to reach his new home. He arrived in Melbourne on Tuesday, November 1, 1949. An overcast day that cleared for the running of the Melbourne Cup in front of a crowd estimated at 110,000. Foxzami, a 16-1 chance, won the race from a field of 31 and won $25,000 in prizemoney. As an International Refugee Association “displaced person”, Chemia Kwiat owed the Commonwealth government two years of compulsory labour and was sent to migrant camps in South Australia, where he spent months living in army Nissen huts, before returning to Melbourne. He was released from compulsory work on Wednesday, November 7, 1951, the day after Delta won the Melbourne Cup. A document from Kwiat’s journey to Australia. National Archives Kwiat applied for citizenship in 1954, was approved the following year, and settled in the suburb of Balaclava. He was no longer a tailor but a storeman working in Little Bourke Street. On August 30, 1959, he married a woman of Greek Orthodox faith and, according to the forensic institute team, stopped practising as a Jew. They had one child. “This is why we found no leads from the Jewish community here because he was not known,” Daniel says. Editor's pick Analysis Naked City The DNA detectives taking on the grim reality of Ukraine’s war The trail became narrower when the forensic team discovered Kwiat’s brothers, Izrael and Yitzhak, had died in Israel. Yitzhak had wanted to maintain links, writing to the Jewish organisations in Melbourne wanting to find his brother. Yitzhak’s relatives said they corresponded for years until Chemia stopped responding to letters. Daniel says they conducted many “wild goose chases” but scouring public records helped find individuals to build the family tree. One lead came through an ad in Israel promoting a man selling tomatoes. The 1972 and 1977 Australian electoral rolls, showed Kwiat and his wife lived together in Carlton North. In 1980, their child was recorded on the same roll. Then there is a blank. Disengaged from his relatives overseas and no longer seeing his wife and child, Kwiat re-emerged in Nicholson Street. His child said they had lost contact 25 years earlier. Was he there because he was familiar with the area or to be close to the wife he no longer saw? His alcove was 350 metres away, a four-minute walk from what had been his home when he lived another life. Editor's pick The Last Word Tragedy The boys from ruined Europe whose dreams died in the Snowy Mountains “We thought there must be a reason why he was living there,” Hartman says. The neighbour, Trevor Lithgow says, “I always felt he felt this was his place.” For the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine team the years of international effort were justified when a coroner was satisfied the unidentified man was Chemia Kwiat. “We lived and breathed the case,” Daniel says. “The neighbours were grateful that he wasn’t forgotten.” “Everyone deserves a name,” says Hartman. “It was nice to see a [passport] photo where he had a smile on his face.” The institute team found that Kwiat’s wife died on May 12, 2004, and was laid to rest at the Melbourne Cemetery just up the road. Eleven days later, Kwiat was found dead in his alcove. The autopsy showed the cause of death was pneumonia, but was it a broken heart? John Silvester lifts the lid on Australia’s criminal underworld. https://www.travelerstoday.com/articles/.text: European tourism is running hotter than ever — and the arguments about what to do with that heat are going to be had publicly, free, and on the record tomorrow. The Euronews Travel and Tourism Summit convenes Tuesday in Brussels with a lineup that puts a sitting prime minister, the head of the world's largest privately held cruise company, aviation-sector leaders, and the EU lawmakers behind Europe's first sustainable tourism strategy all on the same stage in a single day — and anyone can watch.The one-day event at Brussels' Albert Hall opens at 9:00 a.m. local time and runs until 6:00 p.m. It is free to watch live on euronews.com, the Euronews app, and YouTube. For travelers trying to understand where European tourism policy is heading — and what it might mean for where they can go, what they will pay, and how crowded their next trip to Dubrovnik or Barcelona will be — the agenda is unusually substantive.What topics are being debated at the summit?The day opens with Eduardo Santander, chief executive of the European Travel Commission, reviewing the 2026 season — which ended, according to Eurocontrol's Special Summer 2026 Flash Briefing, with Europe recording its busiest summer ever: an average of 35,959 flights per day across July and August, a 2.4% increase on 2025, with a single-day peak of 37,659 flights on July 24.That record demand arrived despite disruption from the ongoing Middle East conflict, which raised fuel costs, closed several air corridors, and rerouted traffic toward continental European alternatives. Albania, Croatia, Cyprus, Greece, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia, and Slovenia all saw what Eurocontrol described as "high increases" in air traffic as travelers pivoted toward destinations perceived as safer and closer to home. France, meanwhile, was responsible for 32% of all air traffic flow management delays across the continent.Sustainability is the summit's dominant thread. Three separate sessions — a panel on shaping the future of travel, a discussion on managing visitor flows, and an East-meets-West connectivity panel — examine different dimensions of the same underlying question: whether the European tourism model needs structural reform rather than incremental adjustment.How does Europe plan to fix overtourism?The most consequential session for ordinary travelers may be the afternoon panel on managing visitor flows and shaping tomorrow's destinations, which includes Mato Franković, the mayor leading Dubrovnik's approach to overtourism.Dubrovnik has gone further than most European cities in quantifying the problem and testing solutions: it limits cruise ships to a daily maximum of two vessels with an 8,000-passenger cap, runs real-time people counters in the historic center, and has a managed arrival booking system aimed at spreading visitors across the year. The conversation at the summit will put that experiment in the context of a broader European policy push.MEP Daniel Attard — the Maltese lawmaker who led the European Parliament's transport and tourism committee through a vote on sustainable tourism policy in March 2026, and who won the 2026 MEP Award for Sustainable Tourism — also appears on the speaker list. His work at the Parliament has framed the coming EU strategy around a stark statistic: 80% of the world's travelers concentrate on just 10% of destinations, a pattern that puts enormous pressure on Venice, Santorini, Barcelona, and a handful of other cities while leaving most European regions starved for visitor spending.MEP Nikolina Brnjac, a Croatian member of the European Parliament's center-right group who is also on the tourism policy file, rounds out the parliamentary contingent. Together, their presence at the summit signals that the policy conversation happening in Brussels corridors and on Brussels stages is more coordinated than it has been at any point in recent memory.The summit does not attempt to translate "second cities" — lesser-known destinations such as Matera in Italy, Plovdiv in Bulgaria, or Kalamata in Greece that tourism bodies have been actively promoting — as a cure-all. Getting travelers to secondary destinations requires real changes in air connectivity, not just marketing. Ourania Georgoutsakou, managing director of Airlines4Europe, the trade body representing major European carriers, is also on the bill.Can MSC Cruises really chart a greener course?One of the summit's most closely watched segments will be The Big Question, a Euronews interview format, in which Euronews journalists will put MSC Cruises CEO Gianni Onorato directly on the record about cruise decarbonization commitments.The cruise industry is under sustained pressure over its environmental footprint. MSC Cruises has committed to reaching net-zero greenhouse-gas emissions from its marine operations by 2050, has expanded shore power connections across more than 15 European ports through 2026, and has deployed LNG-powered ships — including MSC World Europa, equipped with solid oxide fuel cell technology designed to cut emissions further, and MSC Euribia.The session will examine the concept of "blue corridors" — designated shipping routes between major ports where zero-emission or low-emission operations are agreed across all operators, not just individual lines. The viability of such corridors depends on bunkering infrastructure that does not yet exist at scale at most European cruise ports, which is why the conversation typically pivots between ambition and logistics.Expect Onorato to be pressed on the practical timeline — which fuels, which ports, which ships, and what the transition will cost passengers in fares. Those are the questions that determine whether green cruising remains a branding exercise or becomes a structural shift in how cruise itineraries are planned and priced.Why is Albania's prime minister at a travel summit?Edi Rama, Albania's prime minister, sits down for a one-on-one interview with Euronews anchor Maria Tadeo at 1:22 p.m. local time — the longest dedicated slot in the summit's afternoon program.Albania has been Europe's fastest-growing tourism destination for several consecutive years. According to the Euronews preview report, the country welcomed 11.9 million international arrivals in 2025 — a 93.6% increase compared with 2019, according to UN Tourism data — driven by improved air connectivity, affordable prices, and growing interest in the Albanian Riviera, Tirana, and the country's mountain regions.That trajectory raises a question the summit could sharpen: Albania is now being promoted as the answer to overtourism in neighboring Greece and Croatia, but it is already experiencing the early symptoms of the same problem it is supposed to solve. Ksamil, a small coastal town near Saranda, has documented crowding, environmental degradation, and unchecked development — the same pattern that turned parts of Croatia into cautionary tales a decade earlier. Rama is expected to address Albania's strategy for managing growth rather than simply maximizing it.The summit will also hear from Pedro Machado, Portugal's Secretary of State for Tourism, and Dan Adrian Pop, Romania's Secretary of State for digitalization and tourism — both countries navigating the same trade-off between the economic weight of tourism and its costs to residents.How to watch the Euronews summit on TuesdayThe Euronews Travel and Tourism Summit is free to watch. Doors open at 9:00 a.m. Brussels time (3:00 a.m. ET) on Tuesday, September 29, with sessions running until 6:00 p.m. Brussels time (noon ET). The full schedule and livestream details are at euronews.com.The full day is available at euronews.com, on the Euronews app on iOS and Android, and via Euronews' YouTube channel. No registration is required for the livestream.Key sessions to track for travel policy signals:The 10:01 a.m. session with Eduardo Santander (ETC) sets the context for the year's numbers. The 11:19 a.m. Big Question with Gianni Onorato (MSC Cruises) is the cruise industry's highest-profile accountability moment of the year on decarbonization. The 1:22 p.m. Edi Rama interview is the political headline. The 1:53 p.m. panel on managing visitor flows is where the most directly traveler-relevant policy details are likely to emerge. The 4:25 p.m. East Meets West panel on connectivity takes up the question of how Europe and Asia strengthen travel links amid an altered geopolitical map.The Michelin Guide's Marie-France Perrel, head of business development for hotels, closes the formal program at 5:00 p.m., offering a hospitality industry perspective on where quality and sustainability intersect for accommodation.The session most likely to go off-script: The Ring, Euronews' head-to-head debate format, hosted by Méabh Mc Mahon, scheduled for 3:38 p.m. Its topic has not been confirmed in advance — which, given the composition of the speaker list, makes it the segment likeliest to surface the genuine disagreements that conference panels usually paper over.

https://www.hngn.com/articles/273655/202.text: Polish police have detained a 55-year-old Russian citizen on suspicion of spying for a foreign intelligence service after he was filmed photographing trains and railway infrastructure in Świdnica, in the Lower Silesian region of southwestern Poland, and a court has ordered him held for three months while prosecutors build an espionage case, authorities said on Friday. Investigators seized about 250,000 photographs from him, Interior Ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka told a briefing. His name has not been released, and officials did not say which service he is believed to have worked for.The espionage charge carries a minimum sentence of five years under Polish law. The detail that drew comment in Warsaw was the suspect's nationality. "Russia is carrying out hybrid operations against Poland and other" European countries, Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister coordinating Poland's special services, told the broadcaster RMF24, adding that detaining a Russian citizen was atypical of the model Moscow has used in Poland, which has relied overwhelmingly on recruited Ukrainians and Belarusians, often paid small sums over Telegram to photograph sites, spray slogans or carry packages. A Russian national in the field, with a quarter of a million images, suggests either a different kind of operation or a different level of confidence.Railways are the target that makes sense. Poland is the primary logistics corridor for Western military aid to Ukraine, most of it moving by rail toward the Rzeszów hub and the border crossings, and Lower Silesia's lines carry traffic from Germany and the Czech Republic into that network. Polish authorities have attributed a series of rail incidents over the past year, including sabotage of track on the Warsaw–Lublin line, to Russian services, and the country's security agencies said this month that the number of espionage cases opened last year was more than double 2024's, with the two years together exceeding the previous three decades.The arrest is one of several in a month of them. On October 16 military police detained a 31-year-old reservist with Polish and Ukrainian citizenship on espionage suspicion; earlier in October a suspect was charged with reconnaissance of Rzeszów-Jasionka airport as part of what prosecutors described as a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky during a transit through Poland; and in December a Russian national was charged with running an espionage and sabotage network for the FSB whose agents were mainly Ukrainians and Belarusians. Poland has expelled Russian diplomats in waves since 2022 and closed the last Russian consulate on its territory last year. Moscow denies conducting espionage or sabotage in Poland.The Świdnica case will proceed under a classified investigation, as espionage prosecutions in Poland generally do, and the three-month detention order can be extended. Whether the 250,000 photographs show what prosecutors say they show, and whom they were for, is what the next three months will establish.
